review:
## Overview  
Language models trained on corpora with conflicting or low‑quality content often generate outputs that do not align with any part of the training data, producing both extrinsic and intrinsic hallucinations. This phenomenon is a direct consequence of noisy or contradictory data in the training set.  
- Contradictory or noisy training data can confuse semantic understanding and parametric knowledge learning, leading to hallucinations [10].  
- Hallucinations are considered a form of generalization error, arising when a model’s predictions deviate from the ground‑truth function due to imperfect data or training conditions [3].  

## Main approaches  
### Data‑level mitigation  
- Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) incorporates external knowledge at generation time to ground outputs and reduce hallucinations caused by data noise [8].  
- Post‑training data augmentation and cleaning of low‑quality or uncurated corpora are used to improve factual grounding [7][8].  

### Training‑level mitigation  
- Model editing and contrastive learning are applied during fine‑tuning to separate factual from spurious patterns learned from noisy data [8].  
- Reinforcement learning with human or AI feedback (RLHF) is employed to shape model behaviour toward truthfulness, though it can also introduce trade‑offs with safety and factual accuracy [6][8].  

### Inference‑time mitigation  
- Self‑reflection and confidence‑calibration modules can flag uncertain generations, reducing the risk of confident hallucinations that arise from noisy data [8][2].  
- External fact‑checking pipelines are used at generation time to verify the factuality of outputs before they are returned to the user [8].  

### Regularization techniques  
- Temperature scaling, a post‑hoc calibration method, has been shown to improve Expected Calibration Error (ECE) for models, providing a more reliable uncertainty signal that can mitigate hallucinations stemming from noisy training signals [2].  

## How the papers compare  
| Lifecycle stage | Typical methods | Reported impact on hallucination | Key source |
|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------------------------|------------|
| Data | RAG, data cleaning | Improves factual grounding, reduces extrinsic hallucinations | [8] |
| Training | Model editing, contrastive learning, RLHF | Alters internal representations, can reduce both hallucination and safety failures | [8][6] |
| Inference | Self‑reflection, confidence calibration, external fact‑checking | Provides real‑time safeguards, often used as last‑line defense | [8] |
| Calibration | Temperature scaling | Lowers ECE, improves uncertainty estimates | [2] |

The papers emphasize data‑level fixes as the most direct response to noisy training material, whereas training‑ and inference‑time techniques act as complementary safeguards. Calibration methods are applied across stages to improve the reliability of model confidence.  

## Limitations and open problems  
- Many mitigation studies rely on auxiliary systems (retrieval, fact‑checking) that introduce additional infrastructure costs and potential new failure modes [8].  
- The trade‑off between reducing hallucinations and maintaining factual accuracy or safety remains poorly quantified; some interventions that improve truthfulness may inadvertently increase refusal or safety errors [6].  
- Calibration improvements measured by ECE do not guarantee factual correctness, as high confidence can still coincide with hallucinations [5][2].  
- Existing benchmarks (HalluLens, HalluScan, OpenHalDet) evaluate hallucination rates but rarely isolate the effect of noisy versus clean training data, limiting causal conclusions about noise impact [14][13][15].  

## Gaps in the evidence  
- The influence of noisy training data on core performance metrics—accuracy, calibration, and generalization—has limited empirical support; most studies report qualitative or anecdotal findings rather than quantitative benchmarks [10].  
- Effectiveness of specific data‑cleaning or robust regularization strategies against noise is not systematically compared across models or datasets [7][8].  
- Benchmark protocols that dynamically generate test questions and evaluate refusal or abstention are relatively recent and have not yet been standardized for noisy‑data evaluation [14].  
- Cross‑lingual generalizability of noise mitigation techniques remains unexplored, as current studies focus primarily on English datasets and models [13].  

These gaps highlight the need for controlled experiments that systematically vary training‑data noise levels and evaluate corresponding changes in accuracy, calibration, and generalization across diverse benchmark settings.

comparison.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Code Hallucinations in LLMs: Characterization, Mitigation Methods, Challenges, and Future Directions for Reliable AI
comparison.problem: Hallucination in code generation by large language models hampers reliable software engineering tasks.
comparison.method: Systematic literature review of 60 papers, following Kitchenham guidelines, categorizing causes, mitigation, and evaluation.
comparison.data_or_benchmarks: Benchmarks include static metrics and dynamic checks such as compilation and execution correctness.
comparison.key_results: Hallucinations arise from data noise, exposure bias, semantic gaps; mitigated by knowledge‑enhanced decoding, constrained generation, post‑editing; code challenges include syntax, typing, libraries.
comparison.limitations: Few code‑hallucination studies; benchmarks lack unified, hallucination‑aware metrics; challenges in private codebases and balancing reliability with generalization.

comparison.method: Formal definitions, risk bounds via PAC-Bayes and Rademacher, detection (uncertainty, calibration, attention) and mitigation (retrieval, fine-tuning, logit, verification).

comparison.title: HalluLens: LLM Hallucination Benchmark
comparison.problem: LLMs hallucinate, producing content inconsistent with training data, undermining trust and adoption.
comparison.method: Proposed HalluLens benchmark with a clear hallucination taxonomy, new extrinsic tasks, dynamic test generation, and analysis of existing benchmarks.
comparison.data_or_benchmarks: HalluLens comprising three new extrinsic hallucination tasks and three existing intrinsic tasks, with dynamic test set generation.
comparison.key_results: Benchmark evaluates extrinsic hallucinations, resists data leakage, and offers comprehensive analysis separating hallucination from factuality.

comparison.problem: Hallucinations in LLMs: generating factually incorrect or unfaithful content.
comparison.method: Systematic benchmark evaluating hallucination detection across 6 methods, 4 model families, 3 domains.

sources.text: responsible. To address RQ4, this section examines mitigation strategies that aim to reduce or correct hallu- cinations after they occur, analyzing techniques applied at the data, training, and inference stages of the LLM lifecycle. In this survey, mitigation refers to interven- tions designed to reduce, correct, or contain hallucinations after the core model pretraining stage has already occurred. These approaches typically operate during post-training alignment, retrieval augmentation, decoding control, veri- fication, or response correction. Prevention, by contrast, refers to proactive strategies intended to reduce the likelihood of hallucination emer- gence before or during foundational model devel- opment. Preventive approaches primarily focus on improving dataset quality, strengthening train- ing robustness, embedding factual grounding, and introducing structural constraints that reduce hal- lucination risks earlier in the lifecycle pipeline. Although certain techniques such as reinforcement learning through human feedback (RLHF) may exhibit characteristics of both mitigation and pre- vention, this survey categorizes them according to their primary operational role within the lifecycle framework. 5.1 Data-Related Mitigation methods based on data address halluci- nations caused by biased, incomplete or conflicting data. sources.title: Hallucinations in LLMs: A Lifecycle-Based Survey of Causes, Detection, Mitigation, and Prevention
sources.text: that halluci- nation reduction techniques operate at different levels of the LLM lifecycle and exhibit varying trade-offs between effectiveness, computational cost, and generalizability. Data-level mitigation methods such as retrieval-augmented generation and post-training data augmentation primarily improve factual grounding by incorporating exter- nal knowledge or higher-quality training signals. Training-level approaches, including model edit- ing, contrastive learning, and reinforcement learn- ing with human or AI feedback, attempt to modify internal representations to better distin- guish factual and spurious patterns. Inference- time methods such as self-reflection, confidence calibration, and external fact-checking act as run- time safeguards that detect or correct unreliable outputs during generation. However, the analysis also reveals that many mitigation techniques rely on additional infrastructure such as retrieval sys- tems, verification pipelines, or feedback models, which introduces new dependencies and compu- tational costs. Consequently, current mitigation strategies function primarily as corrective mecha- nisms rather than fully eliminating the underlying causes of hallucinations. 6 Prevention of Hallucination Mitigation techniques deal with correcting what has already happened, whereas prevention tech- niques deal with the repression of the appearance of hallucinations at the outset. sources.text: Data-Related: Unseen or Limited Knowledge When the training data lacks relevant information, the model may attempt to fabricate responses to queries, leading to potential extrinsic hallucinations. This issue arises with queries requiring up-to-date knowledge (Kasai et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a; Onoe et al., 2022), involving unanswerable problems (e.g., unsolved scientific problems) (Yin et al., 2023; Amayuelas et al., 2023), and concerning long-tail knowledge (Mallen et al., 2023a; Kandpal et al., 2023). In such cases, LLMs may generate content unsupported by the training data. Ideally, LLMs should recognize the knowledge bourdary, “what they don’t know”, and abstain from providing fabricated content when encountering queries that require such knowledge (Cheng et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2024). Data-Related: ContradictoryorNoisyTrainingDataandInputSource When the training data contains conflicting or noisy information the model may become confused or misled (Carlini et al., 2021). This can challenge semantic understanding and parametric knowledge learning, leading to both extrinsic and intrinsic hallucinations. If the generated content is supported by any part of the training data, it is not considered hallucination, as it aligns with the training data. sources.text: primary metrics to quantify uncertainty. English-only evaluation. Our benchmark is conducted exclusively in English, limiting the generalizability of findings to multilingual or non-English contexts. Hallu- cination patterns may differ substantially across languages, particularly for languages with less training data representation or different linguistic structures. The effective- ness of detection methods may also vary, as NLI models are predominantly trained on English data and may perform poorly on non-English inputs. LLM-as-Judge variance. The LLM-as-Judge detection method relies on the capabilities of the judge model, introducing a source of variance that is difficult to fully control. While we mitigate this through structured evaluation rubrics and position randomization, the judge model itself may exhibit biases or hallucinations that affect evaluation reliability. This limitation is inherent to any evaluation framework that uses LLMs as evaluators and represents a fundamental challenge in the field. Static benchmark assumption. Our benchmark evaluates models on fixed datasets at a single point in time. In practice, LLM hallucination patterns evolve as models are updated, fine-tuned, or deployed with different system prompts. A static benchmark cannot capture these temporal dynamics, and detection methods that perform well on current model outputs may become less effective as models evolve.
